### 1. WHAT IT IS
The **Computer Training Centres (Regulation) Bill, 2004** is a Private Member's Bill introduced in the Lok Sabha by Shri Iqbal Ahmed Saradgi, M.P., to regulate private computer training institutions, mandate registration, enforce quality standards and prescribed fee structures, and penalise institutions operating without statutory compliance [1] [2].

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
- **Proposer / Ownership**: Introduced by **Shri Iqbal Ahmed Saradgi, M.P.** [1].
- **Legal Status**: Private Member's Bill (as-introduced text; not enacted into law) [1] [2].
- **Date of Introduction / Presentation**: **18 August 2004** (dated in New Delhi) [2].

### 3. DESIGN
Under **Clause 10** of the Bill, any person who violates the provisions of the proposed Act faces the following statutory penal stipulations [3]:

| Penalty Component | Stipulated Statutory Requirement |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Minimum Term of Imprisonment** | **Not less than three years** [3] |
| **Maximum Term of Imprisonment** | **Not in record.** (Clause 10 prescribes only the floor of not less than three years) [3] |
| **Minimum Fine** | **Not less than ₹1,00,000** (one lakh rupees) [3] |
| **Maximum Fine** | **Not in record.** (Clause 10 prescribes only the floor of not less than one lakh rupees) [3] |

### 4. TRADE-OFFS
- **Strongest Case For (from the record)**: Protects students from exploitation by unregistered centres that collect exorbitant fees, lack basic facilities and curriculum content, or abruptly shut down operations before completing courses [4].
- **Strongest Case Against (from the record)**: Rigid minimum sentencing floors (a minimum mandatory 3 years' imprisonment and ₹1,00,000 fine) without statutory upper ceilings or judicial discretion could impose disproportionately harsh criminal liability for non-registration [3].

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
- **Registration Authority**: Appropriate Government scrutiny and mandatory registration within one month from commencement [5].
- **Regulatory Enforcement**: Power of the appropriate Government under Clause 9 to investigate complaints within one month and forthwith cancel registrations [3].

### WHAT IT IS
The **Computer Training Centres (Regulation) Bill, 2004** is a Private Member's Bill introduced in Parliament by **Shri Iqbal Ahmed Saradgi, M.P.** to regulate computer training centres, mandate compulsory registration, prescribe syllabi and fee structures, and penalise unregistered or non-compliant operations [1] [2].

### PENAL PROVISIONS (IMPRISONMENT AND FINE)
Under **Clause 10** of the Computer Training Centres (Regulation) Bill, 2004:
* **Minimum Term of Imprisonment:** Imprisonment for a term which **shall not be less than three years** [3].
* **Minimum Fine:** A fine which **shall not be less than one lakh rupees** (₹1,00,000) [3].

The text does not specify an upper statutory cap on either the prison term or the fine in Clause 10, framing both exclusively as mandatory statutory floors [3].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Sponsor / Ownership:** Introduced by Shri Iqbal Ahmed Saradgi, M.P. [2].
* **Appropriate Authority:** Envisaged implementation by the "appropriate Government" (defined as the Central Government or State Government as the case may be) [4].
* **Status:** Introduced legislative proposal; not enacted into law in force.

### DESIGN & COMPLIANCE REQUIREMENTS
* **Mandatory Prior Registration:** Prohibits running any computer centre without prior registration with the appropriate Government [5]. Existing centres were required to apply within **one month** of commencement [5].
* **Standards & Fee Regulation:** The appropriate Government is mandated to prescribe the syllabus and fees for each course imparted by a computer centre [6].
* **Complaints & Deregistration:** Complaints must be investigated with a decision taken within **one month** of receipt; verified complaints result in immediate cancellation of registration [6].

### WHAT IT IS
Under the **Copyright (Second Amendment) Bill, 1992**, the adaptation of a computer programme for debugging purposes was proposed to be permitted by creating a fair dealing exception to copyright infringement and establishing a corresponding restriction on the author's moral rights [1][2][3].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Originating Authority / Ministry:** Ministry of Human Resource Development (introduced by Shri Arjun Singh) [4][5].
* **Chamber & Date of Introduction:** Lok Sabha on **6 July 1992** [5].
* **Status in Record:** Bill as introduced [5].

### STATUTORY DESIGN
The mechanism to permit software debugging comprised two operative statutory provisions:

1. **Fair Dealing Exception under Section 52(1):**
   * Through **Clause 17** of the Bill, a new **clause (aa)** was proposed to be inserted into sub-section (1) of section 52 of the Copyright Act, 1957, providing that the following shall not constitute an infringement of copyright [2][3]:
     > *"(aa) the making of copies of adaptation of a computer programme by the lawful possessor of a copy of such computer programme, from such copy—*
     > *(i) in order to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied; or*
     > *(ii) to make back-up copies purely as a temporary protection against loss, destruction or damage in order only to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied;"* [3]
   * The **Notes on Clauses** (Clause 17) explicitly confirm that this provision was inserted *"to cover the legitimate requirement of the lawful owner of a copy of a computer programme to make adaptations for 'debugging' and to make back-up copies"* [2].

2. **Restriction on Author's Moral Rights under Section 57(1):**
   * Through **Clause 20** of the Bill, an amendment to section 57(1) of the principal Act introduced a specific proviso to prevent authors from restraining or seeking damages for debugging adaptations [1][6]:
     > *"Provided that the author shall not have any right to restrain or claim damages in respect of any adaptation of a computer programme to which clause (aa) of sub-section (1) of section 52 applies."* [6]
   * The **Notes on Clauses** (Clause 20) noted that this proviso was added *"whereby adaptation of a computer programme for the purpose commonly known as 'debugging' is sought to be made permissible"* without exposure to moral rights claims regarding prejudicial distortion or modification [1][6].

### TRADE-OFFS
* **Strongest Case For:** Safeguards bona fide software licensees and lawful possessors from copyright infringement or moral rights litigation when rectifying errors ("debugging") or making protective back-up copies to ensure the software functions as intended [1][2][3].
* **Strongest Case Against:** Broad permissions around software adaptation historically prompted software industry concerns regarding potential code misuse [7][8]. The Bill balanced this by proposing a penal provision under proposed section 63C, which made knowing use of an infringing copy of a computer programme punishable by imprisonment (one month to three years) and fine (₹50,000 to ₹2,00,000) [8].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* Track the final statutory text adopted when these proposals were subsequently legislated in the *Copyright (Amendment) Act, 1994*, which formally inserted section 52(1)(aa) into force in the Copyright Act, 1957.

### 1. WHAT IT IS
Under the **Copyright (Second Amendment) Bill, 1992**, the adaptation of software for "debugging" purposes was addressed through an exception to copyright infringement, paired with a restriction on the author's moral rights [2, 3]. Specifically, the Bill proposed inserting a new **clause (aa)** into **sub-section (1) of section 52** of the Copyright Act, 1957, establishing that the making of copies or adaptation of a computer programme by a lawful possessor from their copy does not constitute infringement if done in order to utilize the programme for the purpose for which it was supplied [3, 8].

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ministry / Custodian:** Ministry of Human Resource Development (introduced in Lok Sabha by Arjun Singh, Minister of Human Resource Development) [33].
* **Instrument Type:** Statutory Bill amending the Copyright Act, 1957 [5].
* **Stage & Date:** Introduced on **6 July 1992** [33].

### 3. DESIGN & PROVISIONS
The legislative framework to permit adaptation for debugging comprised two complementary provisions:

* **Non-Infringing Fair Dealing Exception (Section 52(1)):**
  The Bill sought to insert **clause (aa)** after clause (a) of Section 52(1) to state that the following acts would not constitute copyright infringement [8]:
  > *"(aa) the making of copies of adaptation of a computer programme by the lawful possessor of a copy of such computer programme, from such copy—*
  > *(i) in order to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied; or*
  > *(ii) to make back-up copies purely as a temporary protection against loss, destruction or damage in order only to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied;"* [8]
  
  The *Notes on Clauses* confirm that this new clause (aa) was inserted *"to cover the legitimate requirement of the lawful owner of a copy of a computer programme to make adaptations for 'debugging' and to make back-up copies"* [3, 7].

* **Protection Against Moral Rights Claims (Section 57):**
  To ensure that an author's special moral rights could not block legitimate debugging adaptations, the Bill proposed a proviso to **Section 57(1)** [2, 17]:
  > *"Provided that the author shall not have any right to restrain or claim damages in respect of any adaptation of a computer programme to which clause (aa) of sub-section (1) of section 52 applies."* [17]

### 4. TRADE-OFFS
* **Case For:** Provides legal certainty and protection for bona fide software users and lawful possessors to debug, maintain, and adapt software to make it run for its intended purpose without facing infringement suits or moral rights obstruction from original authors [2, 3].
* **Case Against:** The Bill simultaneously removed computer programmes from the broader general fair-dealing exception for "private study" under Section 52(1)(a) to protect copyright holders against unauthorized copying, and proposed penalizing the knowing use of infringing computer programmes under Section 63C [3, 8, 21].

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Enactment History:** The 1992 amendment proposals for computer programmes later culminated in the passage of the **Copyright (Amendment) Act, 1994**, which formally enacted Section 52(1)(aa) into Indian copyright law (**Not in record** for subsequent legislative debates on the 1994 passage).
* **Subsequent Interoperability Clauses:** Subsequent amendments, such as the Copyright (Amendment) Bill, 1999, introduced further explicit fair dealing exceptions for software interoperability (clause ab) and testing/study of functionality (clause ac) [14].

### WHAT IT IS
The **Special Educational Facilities for Children of Manual Scavengers Bill, 2001** is a private member's legislative proposal introduced in the Rajya Sabha by Shri S.S. Ahluwalia to provide comprehensive free educational facilities (from school through post-graduate, medical, and technical education) to children of scavengers or Safai Karamcharis [1], [2].

### IDENTIFICATION RESPONSIBILITY UNDER THE BILL
Under **Clause 3** of the Bill, the responsibility for identifying eligible beneficiaries is placed on the **appropriate Government** (defined as the State Government in the case of a State, and the Central Government in other cases) [3], [4]:

- **Mandatory Survey**: It is the duty of the appropriate Government to conduct a survey within the area under its jurisdiction to identify the children of scavengers [4].
- **Preparation of List**: The appropriate Government must prepare a list, in such manner as may be prescribed by rules, of such children who are to be imparted education by that Government [4].
- **Periodic Revision**: The appropriate Government is mandated to cause this beneficiary list to be revised at such intervals as may be prescribed [4].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
- **Administrative Enforcement**: Clause 7 provides that the appropriate Government may appoint **Attendance Authorities** (and supporting personnel) to assist in executing the duties and ensuring children attend institutions [5].
- **Financial Burden**: As set out in the Bill's Financial Memorandum, conducting the survey under Clause 3 and delivering the educational entitlements under Clause 4 was estimated to involve a recurring annual expenditure of approximately **₹100 crore** and a non-recurring expenditure of **₹10 crore** from the Consolidated Fund of India [6].

### WHAT IT IS
The **Special Educational Facilities for Children of Manual Scavengers Bill, 2001** is a private member's legislative proposal introduced in the Rajya Sabha by Shri S.S. Ahluwalia [1] [2]. The Bill aims to break hereditary cycles of manual scavenging by securing free, comprehensive education—from school to post-graduate and technical education—along with hostels, books, stationery, uniforms, transport, and scholarships for children of scavengers [3] [4].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Chamber & Instrument:** Rajya Sabha Private Member's Bill (Bill No. LXX of 2001) [1].
* **Appropriate Government Definition:** In relation to a State, the Government of that State; in all other cases, the Central Government (Clause 2(a)) [1].
* **Status:** Introduced text in Parliament; not enacted into law [1].

### STATUTORY RESPONSIBILITY FOR IDENTIFYING BENEFICIARIES
Under **Clause 3** (*"Survey to be conducted by the appropriate Government"*), the Bill assigns the following explicit duties to the appropriate government regarding beneficiary identification [3] [4]:

| Mandated Action | Statutory Provision (Clause 3) |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Jurisdictional Survey** | It is the statutory duty of the appropriate government to conduct a survey across the area under its jurisdiction to find out the children of scavengers [3] [4]. |
| **Preparation of Beneficiary List** | The appropriate government must prepare a list, in such manner as may be prescribed by rules, of such children who are to be imparted education by that government [3] [4]. |
| **Periodic Revision** | The appropriate government is mandated to cause the identification list to be revised at such intervals as may be prescribed [3] [4]. |

### OPERATIONAL AND ADMINISTRATIVE MACHINERY
* **Entitlements (Clause 4):** Once identified, every child born of a scavenger parent is entitled to free education up to the post-graduate and technical level, free hostel boarding, stationery, uniforms, transport, and monthly scholarships in deserving cases [3].
* **Attendance Authorities (Clause 7):** The appropriate government is empowered to appoint Attendance Authorities and necessary assisting personnel to enforce school attendance and ensure children are not diverted into labour [5] [6].
* **Delegated Rule-Making (Clause 9):** The Central Government is vested with the power to frame rules regarding the exact manner of conducting the survey and the revision intervals for the beneficiary list [4] [7].

### Sources of Revenue Credited to the Right to Work Fund

Under **Section 9(3)** of **The Right to Work Bill, 2002**, the following sources of revenue are mandated to be credited to the **Right to Work Fund** [1], [2]:

1. **Government Grants:** All grants made from time to time by the Central Government under **Section 9(2)** as may be required for the purposes of the Act [1], [2].
2. **Voluntary Donations:** All voluntary donations made to the Fund [1], [2] (which, under **Section 11**, qualify for rebate or deductions from income tax payable by the donee as may be prescribed) [2], [3].
3. **Insurance Policy Contributions:** All contributions in respect of the Right to Work Insurance Policy under **Section 10** [1], [2].
4. **Contributions from Employed Beneficiaries:** All sums collected under **Section 12** [1], [2]—which mandates that every citizen who receives work or allowance under the Act must contribute to the Fund at a prescribed rate and for a prescribed period immediately upon securing work or a job (whether provided by the Government or on their own) [4].
5. **Investment Returns:** Any interest, dividend, or other return on any investment made out of any part of the Fund [2].

### WHAT IT IS
The **Right to Work Bill, 2002** was a Private Member's Bill introduced in the Lok Sabha by Shri G. M. Banatwalla to provide every eligible unemployed citizen a statutory right to work or an allowance (not less than ₹200 per week) until work is provided, backed by the establishment of a dedicated **Right to Work Fund** and an insurance scheme [1][4][13].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
- **Instrument**: Private Member's Bill (Lok Sabha Bill introduced in 2002) [4].
- **Administrative Authority**: Central Government [4][13].
- **Status**: Introduced bill / legislative proposal; recommended by the President under Articles 117 and 274 for introduction and consideration [7].

### MANDATED REVENUE SOURCES CREDITED TO THE FUND
Under **Clause 9(3)** of the Right to Work Bill, 2002, the following five sources of revenue are mandated to be credited to the Right to Work Fund [1][3]:

| Source Provision | Mandated Inflow |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Clause 9(3)(a)** | All grants made by the Central Government under sub-section (2) from time to time as required for the purposes of the Act [1][3]. |
| **Clause 9(3)(b)** | All voluntary donations made to the Fund (which qualify for income-tax rebate/deductions under Clause 11) [1][2][3]. |
| **Clause 9(3)(c)** | All contributions in respect of the Right to Work Insurance Policy under section 10 [1][3]. |
| **Clause 9(3)(d)** | All sums collected under **Section 12** (mandatory contributions from every citizen who receives work or allowance under the Act, for a prescribed period immediately after securing any work or job, whether provided by the Government or on their own, at prescribed rates) [1][3][21]. |
| **Clause 9(3)(e)** | Any interest, dividend, or other return on any investment made out of any part of the Fund [3]. |

### TRADE-OFFS & FINANCIAL DESIGN
- **Strongest Case in Record**: Creates a self-replenishing, hybrid financing mechanism combining budgetary outlays with voluntary donations, insurance mechanisms, and post-employment contributions from beneficiaries once they secure work, reducing recurring state expenditure over time [2][8][33].
- **Pressure Points / Gaps**: The Financial Memorandum estimated an initial recurring burden of approximately ₹500 crore per annum on the Consolidated Fund of India, depending heavily on the subsequent receipt of insurance contributions and beneficiary recovery under Section 12 [8][33].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
- Prescribing of contribution rates and collection mechanisms under Section 12 via rules under Clause 15(2)(d) [19][21].
- Operational design and underwriting rules for the Right to Work Insurance Policy under Section 10 [1][19].
- Annual reporting to each House of Parliament under Section 14 on Fund administration [5].

### **WHAT IT IS**
Under the **Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Bill, 2004** (enacted as the Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Act, 2007, inserting Part IXB into the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958) [1], [2], a **"recognised security organisation"** is defined under proposed **Section 344K(f)** [1]. To qualify as a recognised security organisation, an entity must satisfy two statutory criteria [1], [2]:
1. **Form and Expertise**: It must be an organisation, company, firm, or body of individuals having expertise in matters relating to security and knowledge of ship and port operations [1], [2].
2. **Official Authorization**: It must be authorised by the Central Government by notification in the Official Gazette to carry out assessment, verification, approval, or certification required by Part IXB or by the International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) Code [1], [2].

### **OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS**
* **Ministry / Government**: Central Government (Ministry of Shipping, Road Transport and Highways) [1], [2].
* **Statutory Form**: Statutory amendment to the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 (inserted as Part IXB, Section 344K(f)) [1], [2].
* **Stage & Passage**: Introduced on **23 December 2004**; passed by the Lok Sabha on **14 August 2007** and by the Rajya Sabha on **6 September 2007**; received Presidential Assent on **24 September 2007** as Act No. 40 of 2007 [1], [2].

### **DESIGN & ROLE**
* **Functions Authorized**: Carrying out assessments, verifications, approvals, or certifications required by Part IXB or the International Ship and Port Facility Security Code [2].
* **Delegated Security Measures**: Under the proviso to **Section 344M(2)**, the Central Government may authorise any recognised security organisation to carry out any of the security measures under Section 344M on its behalf, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed [3].

### WHAT IT IS
Under the **Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Bill, 2004** (enacted as the Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Act, 2007, inserting Part IXB into the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958), a **"recognised security organisation"** is defined under proposed **Section 344K(f)** [1], [2].

### QUALIFICATIONS & DESIGNATION REQUIREMENTS
To qualify and be designated as a recognised security organisation by the Central Government, an entity must satisfy the following statutory criteria under Section 344K(f) [1], [2]:

* **Form of Entity:** It must be any organisation, company, firm, or body of individuals [1], [2].
* **Substantive Expertise & Knowledge:** It must possess:
  1. **Expertise in matters relating to security**, and
  2. **Knowledge of ship and port operations** [1], [2].
* **Statutory Designation / Authorisation:** It must be authorised by the Central Government by notification published in the Official Gazette [1], [2].
* **Scope of Functions:** It is authorised to carry out assessment, verification, approval, or certification required under Part IXB of the Act or by the International Code for the Security of Ships and Port Facilities (ISPS Code) [2].

### DELEGATED POWERS
Under the proviso to proposed **Section 344M(2)**, the Central Government is empowered to authorise any recognised security organisation to carry out any of the security measures under Section 344M on its behalf, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed [25].

### WHAT IT IS
Under the National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill, 2004, the standard workday duration that the State Government must consider when fixing the piece-rate schedule of rates for unskilled manual workers is **seven hours** [1].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Authority:** The State Government fixes the schedule of rates for different types of work every year in consultation with the State Employment Guarantee Council [1].
* **Statutory Provision:** **Schedule I, Paragraph 8** (read alongside **Section 4(3)** and **Schedule I, Paragraph 7**) of the Bill [1], [2], [3].

### DESIGN
* **Piece-Rate Linkage:** When wages are directly tied to the quantity of work executed, payment must follow the schedule of rates established annually by the State Government [1].
* **Benchmarking Metric:** Under **Paragraph 8 of Schedule I**, the schedule of rates of wages for unskilled labourers must be calibrated such that a person working for **seven hours** would normally earn a wage equal to the statutory daily wage rate [1].
* **Absolute Floor:** **Paragraph 6 of Schedule I** explicitly mandates that under no circumstances shall labourers be paid less than the statutory wage rate [1].

### TRADE-OFFS
* **Strongest Case For (Worker Protection):** Anchoring piece-rate task norms to seven hours prevents public works administrators from inflating physical output requirements to depress effective daily remuneration below minimum standards [1].
* **Strongest Case Against (Administrative/Fiscal Rigidity):** Applying a fixed seven-hour wage-equivalence norm across varying terrains and hard-soil conditions restricts the state's discretion to align productivity norms strictly with local commercial contracting rates [1].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Annual Rate Revisions:** Review State Government gazette notifications fixing the annual Schedule of Rates in consultation with the State Council [1].
* **Workday vs. Measurement Audits:** Track public muster rolls and measurement books to ensure tasks calculated for a seven-hour period do not mandate extended hours on site to achieve the statutory wage rate [1].

### **WHAT IT IS**
Under the National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill, 2004 (subsequently enacted as the National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005), when wages are directly linked with the quantity of work done (piece-rate basis), the schedule of rates fixed by the State Government must ensure that an unskilled labourer working for **seven hours** normally earns a wage equal to the statutory daily wage rate [1].

### **OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS**
* **Ministry:** Ministry of Rural Development, Government of India (with implementation decentralized across State Governments, District Programme Coordinators, and Gram Panchayats) [1], [2].
* **Legal Authority:** Schedule I, Paragraph 8 read with Section 4(3) of the legislation [1], [3].
* **Instrument:** Statutory mandate governing state employment guarantee schemes [1], [3].

### **DESIGN & PIECE-RATE BENCHMARK**
| Metric / Parameter | Statutory Specification |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Standard Workday Duration** | **7 hours** [1] |
| **Rate Determinant** | Schedule of rates fixed annually by the State Government in consultation with the State Employment Guarantee Council [1] |
| **Statutory Floor** | Piece-rates must be set such that 7 hours of standard manual work normally yields an amount at least equal to the wage rate; under no circumstances may workers receive less than the notified wage rate [1] |
| **Wage Rate Benchmark** | Fixed by the Central Government (not less than ₹60 per day), or defaulting to the agricultural minimum wage fixed under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 [3] |

### **TRADE-OFFS**
* **Case for the 7-hour Piece-Rate Standard:** Ensures fair compensation for piece-work tasks without subjecting manual laborers to exploitative workdays to meet basic daily subsistence wage levels [1].
* **Case Against / Operational Pressure:** Output norms vary across soil conditions, topography, and seasonal temperatures, risking administrative disputes if standard 7-hour task outputs are overestimated by state public works schedules [1].

### **IMPLEMENTATION WATCH**
* **Schedule Revision Tracking:** Periodic annual updates of state Schedule of Rates (SoR) by State Employment Guarantee Councils to adjust work outputs for varying terrain conditions [1].
* **Payment Verification:** Work measurement windows to avoid delays past the statutory fortnightly disbursement limit [2].

### **WHAT IT IS**
Under the **Institutes of Technology (Amendment) Bill, 2001**, the University of Roorkee was converted into the **Indian Institute of Technology, Roorkee** [1]. To prevent governance disruptions during the structural transition, transitional arrangements were inserted into Section 38 of the Institutes of Technology Act, 1961, governing preexisting authorities until statutory IIT bodies were constituted [2].

---

### **INTERIM ARRANGEMENTS FOR THE ACADEMIC COUNCIL**
Clause 6 of the Bill inserts clause (f) into Section 38 of the principal Act, laying down the interim framework for Roorkee's academic authority [2]:

* **Continuation of Powers:** The Academic Council of the University of Roorkee functioning immediately before the commencement of the Act continues to function as such until a new Senate is constituted for IIT Roorkee under the Act [3].
* **Cessation of Office:** Upon the constitution of the new Senate under the Act, the members of the Academic Council holding office immediately prior to such constitution cease to hold office [3].
* **Application of Statutes and Ordinances:** Under Section 38(g), until the first Statutes and Ordinances for IIT Roorkee are formally framed under the Act, the Statutes and Ordinances of IIT Bombay in force immediately prior to the commencement of the Amendment Act apply to IIT Roorkee with necessary adaptations and modifications, provided they are not inconsistent with the Act [4].

### WHAT IT IS
Under the **Institutes of Technology (Amendment) Bill, 2001**, the University of Roorkee was incorporated into the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) framework as the Indian Institute of Technology, Roorkee [1][2]. The Bill inserted transitional provisions into the principal Act to ensure uninterrupted academic administration and institutional continuity during the conversion process [1][3].

### INTERIM ARRANGEMENTS FOR THE ACADEMIC COUNCIL
According to **Clause 6** of the Bill (inserting clause `(f)` into section 38 of the principal Act):
* **Continuation of Functions:** The **Academic Council of the University of Roorkee**, functioning as such immediately prior to the commencement of the Act, is authorized to continue functioning until a new Senate is formally constituted for IIT Roorkee under the Act [1].
* **Cessation of Office:** Upon the formal constitution of the new Senate under the Act, the members of the Roorkee University Academic Council holding office immediately before such constitution automatically **cease to hold office** [1].
* **Applicability of Rules:** In the transitional interim until the first Statutes and Ordinances are framed for IIT Roorkee, the Statutes and Ordinances of **IIT Bombay** (in force immediately prior to commencement) apply to IIT Roorkee with necessary adaptations, provided they are not inconsistent with the Act [4].

### WHAT IT IS
The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (**TRAI**) initiated a public consultation to design and operationalise an integrated single emergency contact architecture for India [1]. The framework, known as the Integrated Emergency Communication & Response System (**IECRS**), aimed to streamline access to emergency services across the country through a unified number [1].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Authority**: Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (**TRAI**) [1].
* **Recipient / Policy Department**: Department of Telecommunications (**DoT**), Ministry of Communications & IT [1], [2].
* **Issuance Date of Consultation Paper**: **15 March 2013** [1].
* **Status / Instrument Stage**: Consultation paper issued suo-motu by TRAI under the title *'Universal Single Number Based Integrated Emergency Communication & Response System'* on **15 March 2013**; recommendations finalised and submitted to DoT on **7 April 2015** [1], [2].

### DESIGN
* **Instrument Title**: *Universal Single Number Based Integrated Emergency Communication & Response System* [1].
* **Core Objective**: Facilitate the establishment of a robust, pan-India emergency communication and response system accessible via a single emergency number [1].
* **Institutional Stakeholders**: The consultation involved formal discussions and meetings with the Ministry of Home Affairs (**MHA**), the National Disaster Management Authority (**NDMA**), and various State Governments [1].
* **Culmination**: Following stakeholder comments and analysis, TRAI finalised and sent its recommendations on *'Single Number based Integrated Emergency Communication & Response System (IECRS)'* to the DoT on **7 April 2015** [1], [2].

### TRADE-OFFS
* **Arguments for Implementation**: Establishes an efficient, centralised distress mechanism for citizens, replacing disjointed helpline systems [1].
* **Specific Counter-arguments / Disadvantages**: **Not in record.**

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* Operationalisation and integration of emergency control rooms across States by the Ministry of Home Affairs and DoT pursuant to TRAI's recommendations [1], [2].

### **WHAT IT IS**
The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) issued a consultation paper titled **‘Universal Single Number Based Integrated Emergency Communication & Response System’** to facilitate the establishment of an efficient and robust Integrated Emergency Communication & Response System (IECRS) across India [1].

### **OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS**
* **Authority:** Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) [1].
* **Action / Stage:** *Suo-motu* consultation paper issued on **15 March 2013** [1].
* **Subsequent Status:** Following consultations and stakeholder inputs, TRAI finalized and forwarded its recommendations on **“Single Number based Integrated Emergency Communication & Response System (IECRS)”** to the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) on **7 April 2015** [1], [2].

* **Consultation Date:** **15 March 2013** [1].

### WHAT IT IS
Following the sudden discontinuance of its telecom services pursuant to an order of the Supreme Court dated **15 February 2013**, **M/s Unitech Wireless (Tamilnadu) Private Limited** approached the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) to facilitate porting for its subscribers in Mumbai who could not generate a Unique Porting Code (UPC) via normal automated SMS [1].

### SPECIAL CHANNELS PROPOSED
In its letter dated **19 February 2013**, Unitech Wireless requested TRAI to facilitate port outs via a special porting mechanism where it proposed accepting requests for UPC generation through three specific channels [1]:

1. **Call centre** [1]

### 1. WHAT IT IS
**The Special Educational Facilities for Children of Manual Scavengers Bill, 2001** (Bill No. LXX of 2001) is a Private Member's Bill introduced in the Rajya Sabha by Shri S. S. Ahluwalia [1, 3]. It was formulated to provide special educational facilities to children born of scavengers or Safai Karamcharis who were in the past engaged in or employed for manually carrying human excreta in India [1]. Its primary objective is to break the cycle of hereditary manual scavenging and tackle high illiteracy rates by ensuring end-to-end free schooling, higher technical and professional education, living subsidies, and dedicated attendance oversight [2, 7, 24].

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Proposer / Sponsor:** Shri S. S. Ahluwalia, M.P. (Private Member's Bill) [3].
* **Chamber & Bill ID:** Rajya Sabha; Bill No. LXX of 2001 [1].
* **Stage & Status:** As introduced in the Rajya Sabha (not enacted into law) [1].
* **Extent and Commencement:** Extends to the whole of India; designed to come into force at once upon enactment [1].
* **Administrative Ministry:** **Not in record.** (Private Member's Bill).

### 3. DESIGN

#### Key Definitions (Clause 2)
* **Appropriate Government [Clause 2(a)]:** The State Government in the case of a State, and the Central Government in other cases [1].
* **Attendance Authority [Clause 2(b)]:** Attendance Authorities appointed under section (clause) 7 [1].
* **Parent [Clause 2(c)]:** Includes a guardian and every person who has the actual custody of the child of a scavenger [20].
* **Scavenger [Clause 2(e)]:** A person who had been engaged or employed for manually carrying human excreta before the commencement of the *Employment of Manual Scavengers and Construction of Dry Latrines (Prohibition) Act, 1993* (46 of 1993) [20, 22].

#### Key Clauses
* **Survey of Beneficiary Children (Clause 3):** Places a duty on the appropriate Government to conduct a survey across its jurisdiction to identify children of scavengers, prepare a prescribed list of children who are to be imparted education, and revise the list at prescribed intervals [2, 22, 24].
* **Statutory Educational Facilities (Clause 4):** Mandates the appropriate Government to provide every child born of a scavenger parent with:
  * Free education from school level to post-graduate level, including higher medical and technical education [24].
  * Free hostel facilities, uniforms, books, stationery, transportation, and other required educational assistance [24].
  * Monthly scholarships in deserving cases at prescribed rates during their studies [24].
* **Parental Obligation (Clause 5):** Establishes an affirmative duty on the scavenger parent of every child to cause the child to attend an approved school, college, or institution [24, 28].
* **Prohibition on Employing Children (Clause 6):** Enacts a bar stipulating that no person shall employ a child of a scavenger in a manner that prevents the child from attending a school or educational institution [28].
* **Special Provision for Economic Hardship (Clause 8):** If the Attendance Authority is satisfied that a scavenger parent's child cannot attend school or college due to economic or familial circumstances, it may permit the child, by order and subject to conditions, to attend an approved part-time school or institution [6].
* **Delegated Rule-Making Power (Clause 9):** Empowers the Central Government to make rules by notification in the Official Gazette to carry out the purposes of the Act [3, 6].

#### Who Administers It (Clause 7)
* **Attendance Authorities:** Under Clause 7, the appropriate Government (the State Government for a State, the Central Government for Union territories) is empowered to appoint Attendance Authorities and to appoint necessary personnel to assist them in discharging their duties [1, 28].

#### Estimated Outlay (Financial Memorandum)
* **Recurring Expenditure:** Estimated at approximately **₹100 crore** per annum from the Consolidated Fund of India [2].
* **Non-Recurring Expenditure:** Estimated at **₹10 crore** [2].

### 4. TRADE-OFFS
* **Strongest Case For (Statement of Objects and Reasons):** The Statement highlights that despite the *Employment of Manual Scavengers and Construction of Dry Latrines (Prohibition) Act, 1993*, prohibitive laws alone cannot root out manual scavenging because the practice remains hereditary, driven by poverty, and perpetuated by illiteracy [7, 41]. Comprehensive state-funded education up to technical and medical degrees—paired with hostel and transport facilities—is framed as the indispensable prerequisite for social upliftment and alternative livelihood generation [2, 41].
* **Strongest Case Against & Penalties:**
  * **Penalties:** **Not in record.** Unlike the 1993 and 2013 manual scavenging statutes, the 2001 Bill specifies no penal consequences (no fines or imprisonment terms) for employers violating Clause 6 or for non-compliance with Attendance Authority orders.
  * **Enforcement Gaps:** Placing statutory duties on parents (Clause 5) without support structures or clear enforcement remedies risks leaving attendance mandates largely declaratory.

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Subsequent Statutory Framework:** Compare against the subsequently enacted *Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act, 2013*, which codified strict penal sanctions under Section 8 (up to 2 years imprisonment, fine up to ₹1 lakh, or both) [43, 45].
* **Targeted Dependents' Welfare Schemes:** Track existing central interventions including pre-matric scholarships for children of persons involved in hazardous/unclean occupations, capital subsidies, and skill training programmes under the Self Employment Scheme for Rehabilitation of Manual Scavengers (SRMS) [17, 44].

### 1. WHAT IT IS
The **Prevention of Money-Laundering Bill, 1999** was introduced in Parliament to create a comprehensive legal framework to prevent money-laundering, confiscate property derived from or involved in money-laundering, and implement international commitments [2, 9]. These international drivers included the United Nations Convention Against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances, the 1989 Basel Statement of Principles, the 40 recommendations of the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), and the Political Declaration and Global Programme of Action adopted by the UN General Assembly Special Sessions in 1990 and 1998 [7, 18, 34]. It succeeded an earlier draft (The Prevention of Money-laundering Bill, 1998) after incorporating recommendations of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Finance [1, 9].

---

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ministry / Government Ownership:** Central Government (enacted subsequently via the Ministry of Law and Justice / Ministry of Finance) [9, 15, 26].
* **Statutory vs Executive:** Primary statutory legislation [7].
* **Stage and History:** 
  * Introduced originally as the 1998 Bill on **4 August 1998** and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, which presented its report on **4 March 1999** to the Lok Sabha and laid it on the table of the Rajya Sabha on **8 March 1999** [1, 9].
  * The revised legislative initiative was referred to a Select Committee of the Rajya Sabha (report presented **24 July 2000**) and ultimately enacted as **The Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 (Act No. 15 of 2003)** [1, 2].

---

### 3. DESIGN

#### Key Objectives
* Criminalise the laundering of proceeds derived from scheduled offences [14, 52].
* Enable attachment, adjudication, and confiscation of proceeds of crime [19, 56].
* Mandate maintenance and reporting of transaction records by banking companies, financial institutions, and intermediaries [26, 52].
* Establish reciprocal international arrangements for cross-border assistance, asset transfers, and extradition [10, 18, 22].

#### Key Clauses & Institutional Mechanics
| Mechanism / Section | Legal Provision / Design |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Offence of Money-Laundering** (Section 3) | Whosoever directly or indirectly attempts to indulge, knowingly assists, is a party to, or is actually involved in any process or activity connected with the proceeds of crime and projecting it as untainted property [14, 19]. |
| **Attachment & Adjudication** (Sections 5–8) | Empowers the Director/authorised officers to provisionally attach property involved in money-laundering; Adjudicating Authority issues notices, hears parties, and records findings to confirm attachment [27, 55, 56]. |
| **Reporting & Recordkeeping** (Sections 12–15) | Obligates banking companies, financial institutions, and intermediaries to maintain and furnish transaction records under procedures prescribed in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India; fine powers vested in the Director for non-compliance [26]. |
| **Investigative Powers** (Sections 16–24) | Grants survey powers, search and seizure of premises/vehicles/aircraft, search of persons, arrest powers, and retention of records/property [26, 27]. |
| **Burden of Proof** (Section 24) | Reverses the burden of proof onto the accused to prove that proceeds of crime are untainted property [46]. |

#### Penalties
* **General Punishment (Section 4):** Rigorous imprisonment for a minimum term of **3 years**, extendable up to **7 years**, along with a fine extendable up to **₹5 lakh** [14, 19].
* **Enhanced Punishment (Section 4 Proviso):** Where the proceeds of crime relate to offences specified under Paragraph 2 of Part A of the Schedule (drug offences under NDPS framework), imprisonment may extend up to **10 years** [19, 34].

#### Who Administers It
* **Enforcement Directorate / Investigative Director:** Directed by the Director, Assistant Director (appointed under Section 49), and subordinate officers authorised to conduct searches, seizures, arrests, and initiate attachment [24, 27, 45].
* **Adjudicating Authority:** Appointed under Section 6 to confirm provisional attachments and adjudicate property involvement [10, 24, 55].
* **Appellate Tribunal:** Established under Section 25 to hear appeals against Adjudicating Authority orders [24, 52].
* **Special Courts:** Sessions Courts designated under Section 43 to conduct trials for money-laundering offences and decide final confiscation/release [14, 47, 52].

### 4. TRADE-OFFS
* **Strongest Case For (Record):** Protects the integrity and sovereignty of the financial system against transnational organised crime and drug trafficking; complies with FATF 40 recommendations and binding UN resolutions [2, 18, 34].
* **Strongest Case Against / Criticisms (Record):** Reversal of the burden of proof onto the accused under Section 24 [46], strict twin-condition bail restrictions (which the government later proposed relaxing for minors under 16, women, the sick or infirm) [22], and extensive executive search, seizure, and attachment powers vested in the Director [27].

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Inter-Agency Assistance Obligations:** Coordination under Section 54 with sectoral regulators, including RBI, stock exchanges, and subsequent additions (SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA) [26, 41, 51].
* **Cross-Border Reciprocity:** Tracking letters of request, extradition processes, and asset repatriation with foreign jurisdictions under reciprocal agreements [10, 22, 50].
* **Financial Burden:** Ongoing compliance verification and penalty enforcement for reporting non-compliance by banks and non-banking financial entities [26, 52].

### 1. WHAT IT IS
**The Prevention of Money Laundering Bill, 1999** was introduced to establish a comprehensive statutory regime to prevent money laundering and enable the attachment and confiscation of property derived from or involved in money laundering [1, 2]. Designed to give domestic legislative effect to the UN General Assembly Special Session Political Declaration of 8–10 June 1998, Resolution S-17/2 (23 February 1990), and the FATF 40 Recommendations, it targeted illicit drug proceeds and serious crime financing [2, 3, 4]. It served as the direct legislative text that was subsequently enacted into law as the **Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002** (Act No. 15 of 2003) [1].

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Administration**: Empowers the **Central Government** to appoint enforcement and adjudicating authorities and frame rules [5, 6]. The specific administrative ministry in the text of the Bill is **Not in record**.
* **Statutory Nature & Territorial Scope**: A primary parliamentary statute extending to the **whole of India** [2].
* **Legislative Trajectory**:
  * *Predecessor*: The *Prevention of Money-laundering Bill, 1998* was introduced in the Lok Sabha on **4 August 1998** and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance (report presented **4 March 1999**) [7].
  * Reintroduced incorporating committee changes as the 1999 Bill, then referred to a Select Committee of the Rajya Sabha (report presented **24 July 2000**) [8].
  * Enacted as Act No. 15 of 2003 with presidential assent [1].

### 3. KEY CLAUSES & STATUTORY DESIGN

| Instrument / Mechanism | Provision | Statutory Mandate |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Definition of Offence** | Section 3 | Whosoever directly or indirectly attempts to indulge, knowingly assists, is a party to, or is actually involved in any process or activity connected with proceeds of crime and projecting it as untainted property commits money laundering [9, 10]. |
| **Attachment of Property** | Section 5 | The Director (or an officer not below Deputy Director authorized by him) may provisionally attach proceeds of crime for up to **90 days** where a person is charged with a scheduled offence and disposal is anticipated [11, 12]. |
| **Adjudicating Authority** | Sections 6 & 8 | A three-member bench (Chairperson and two Members across law, administration, finance, or accountancy) [13] issues a show-cause notice of not less than **30 days** before confirming attachment and ordering confiscation by the Central Government [14]. |
| **Obligations of Entities** | Sections 12–15 | Banks, financial institutions, and intermediaries must maintain records of specified transactions for **10 years** and furnish reports to the Director [15, 16]. |
| **Survey, Search & Arrest** | Sections 16–18 | Empowers the Director and subordinate officers to inspect premises, search buildings/vehicles/aircraft, seize records, and arrest suspects [17, 18]. |
| **Presumption & Burden of Proof** | Sections 23 & 24 | Presumes inter-connected transactions form part of money laundering [19]; explicitly places the **burden of proving** that proceeds are untainted on the accused [20, 21]. |
| **Appellate Tribunal** | Sections 25–42 | Appeals against orders of the Adjudicating Authority or Director must be preferred within **45 days** [22, 23]. Subsequent appeals lie to the High Court within **60 days** on questions of law or fact [24, 25]. Section 41 bars civil court jurisdiction [24, 25]. |
| **Special Courts** | Sections 43–44 | The Central Government, in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court, designates **Courts of Session** as Special Courts to try Section 4 offences and scheduled offences committed within the area [26, 27]. |
| **The Schedule** | Section 2(y) & Schedule | **Part A** includes offences under the Indian Penal Code (IPC Sections 121, 121A) and the NDPS Act, 1985 (Paragraph 2) [28, 29]. **Part B** includes specified IPC offences (e.g., Sections 302, 304, 307, 308, 327, 329) [30], which constitute scheduled offences only if the total value involved is **₹30 lakh or more** [31]. |

### 4. PENALTIES
* **Substantive Offence (Section 4)**:
  * Rigorous imprisonment for a term between **3 years and 7 years**, and liable to a fine extending up to **₹5 lakh** [9, 10].
  * *Enhanced Penalty*: Where the proceeds of crime relate to offences specified under **Paragraph 2 of Part A of the Schedule** (NDPS Act), the maximum imprisonment is enhanced to **10 years** [10, 28].
* **Reporting Failures (Section 13)**: The Director is empowered to impose fines on banking companies, financial institutions, or intermediaries for non-compliance with record-keeping or reporting duties [15, 16].

### 5. ADMINISTRATION MACHINERY
* **Enforcement Hierarchy (Section 48)**: Administered by the following authorities [6, 32]:
  1. Director or Additional Director or Joint Director
  2. Deputy Director
  3. Assistant Director
  4. Other classes of officers appointed for the Act.
* **Appointment Powers (Section 49)**: 
  * The **Central Government** appoints authorities as it thinks fit under Section 49(1) [5, 6].
  * Central Government may authorize the Director or Additional/Joint/Deputy/Assistant Directors to appoint authorities below the rank of Assistant Director under Section 49(2) [6].
* **Investigative Powers (Section 50)**: The Director exercises civil court powers under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 for discovery, inspection, enforcing attendance, examining on oath, and compelling the production of records [33].
